stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Linguists have long assumed that whistled languages, which turn speech into shifting pitches that carry across valleys, can transmit only brief, formulaic messages such as greetings and warnings. Recordings made by phonologist Ana Ferreira-Klein in the Canary Islands complicate that view. Most of the whistled exchanges she captured were indeed short and predictable. Many others ______ lasting several minutes, these exchanges included jokes, directions, and unscripted arguments.
explanation: There are two complete sentences here: 'Many others were not' and 'lasting several minutes, these exchanges included jokes, directions, and unscripted arguments.' The strong break has to go between them, and that is a grammar question. Where 'however' goes is a logic question. The contrast is with the previous sentence: most exchanges were short, but many others were not. 'However' therefore belongs to the first clause, set off by a comma and followed by the semicolon. The clause after the semicolon doesn't contrast with 'were not' at all. It explains it, by describing how long and varied those exchanges were.

A.why: You applied the rule 'semicolon before however' without checking what 'however' contrasts. This version is grammatical, but it sets up a contrast between 'many others were not [short]' and 'lasting several minutes, these exchanges included jokes...'. Those two ideas agree, because the second explains the first. The real contrast is with the previous sentence, so 'however' has to stay with 'were not.'

B.why: You ran two complete sentences together with no punctuation at all. 'Many others were not' can stand alone, and so can 'lasting several minutes, these exchanges included...'. A long sentence doesn't fix a missing boundary, and 'however' can't join clauses.

D.why: You treated 'however' like 'but' and joined two complete sentences with commas alone. 'However' is an adverb, not a conjunction, so this is a comma splice. One of the two commas has to be a semicolon or period.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Training for several weeks at high altitude reliably raises an endurance athlete's red blood cell count, since thin air prompts the kidneys to release more of the hormone erythropoietin. The method's payoff in competition, which is difficult to measure because most major races are held near sea level, where the added cells begin to disappear within days ______ remains far less certain.
explanation: Cross out the interrupter that opens with the comma after 'competition': 'which is difficult to measure because most major races are held near sea level, where the added cells begin to disappear within days.' What's left is 'The method's payoff in competition ... remains far less certain.' That is one clause, with the subject before the blank and the verb 'remains' after it. Nothing at the blank can be a strong break. You need a comma to close the interrupter and a comma after 'however,' which sits inside the clause and contrasts it with the first sentence.

A.why: You saw 'however' and put a semicolon in front of it, as if two sentences met here. But everything before the blank is a subject plus a long modifier, with no main verb, so a semicolon leaves a fragment on the left and cuts the subject off from 'remains.'

C.why: You put the semicolon after the transition, which attaches 'however' to the wrong side. Neither side can stand alone: the left has no main verb, and 'remains far less certain' has no subject. The semicolon breaks one sentence in two.

D.why: You noticed that an interruption had to close here but used the wrong mark. The interrupter opened with a comma after 'competition,' and the marks around an interruption have to match. A dash can't close what a comma opened.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Engineers testing a new nickel alloy for turbine blades expected the finest-grained samples to resist cracking longest, since smaller grains usually block the spread of microscopic flaws. The samples that endured the most heating cycles before ______ were the coarse-grained ones, a result the team traced to how slowly oxygen moved along their fewer grain boundaries.
explanation: Cross out the transition and reread: 'The samples that endured the most heating cycles before failing were the coarse-grained ones.' That is one sentence. Its subject is 'The samples that endured the most heating cycles before failing' and its verb is 'were.' The two sentences meet at the period after 'flaws,' so the blank has no clause boundary in it. Here 'however' just interrupts a single clause, between its subject and its verb, so it takes a comma on each side. It still marks the contrast with what the engineers expected.

B.why: You used the rule 'semicolon before however' without checking either side. 'The samples that endured the most heating cycles before failing' has no verb of its own, so it can't come before a semicolon. Neither can 'however, were the coarse-grained ones.' The rule only applies when the transition sits between two complete sentences, and here it doesn't.

C.why: This semicolon also has a fragment on each side, because it splits the subject from its verb 'were.' Dropping the comma after 'however' doesn't fix that. It only makes the interruption less clear.

D.why: Moving the semicolon after 'however' still cuts the subject off from its verb. Neither 'The samples...before failing however' nor 'were the coarse-grained ones...' can stand alone, and the transition is left without the commas that set it off.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Earlier studies had found that fiber supplements did little to curb appetite in adults. Participants in the new trial, who ate whole oats rather than taking a powdered supplement, reported feeling noticeably fuller after ______ several also began eating smaller portions without being instructed to.
explanation: There are two complete sentences here: 'Participants...reported feeling noticeably fuller after meals' and 'several also began eating smaller portions.' So a semicolon has to go between them. Now ask which clause 'however' belongs to. Feeling fuller contrasts with the earlier finding that fiber did little for appetite, so 'however' goes with the first clause. Eating smaller portions doesn't contrast with feeling fuller. It adds to it, and 'also' already marks that. So the semicolon goes after 'however.'

A.why: This is the trap that remains after you've spotted the two sentences. You put the semicolon before 'however' out of habit, which makes 'however' point to the second clause. That says eating smaller portions contrasts with feeling fuller, but they agree. The real contrast is with the earlier studies.

C.why: Commas on both sides of 'however' leave the two complete sentences joined by commas alone, which is a comma splice. 'However' is not a conjunction like 'but,' so it can't join sentences.

D.why: This joins two complete sentences with only a comma after 'however,' which is a comma splice. The missing comma before 'however' also leaves it unclear which clause the word belongs to.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Thanks to a decade of wetter-than-average winters, the coastal aquifer refilled faster than hydrologists' models had predicted. Its water had grown steadily ______ chloride readings at the wells nearest the shore had doubled since monitoring began.
explanation: The trailing 'though' means 'however.' It contrasts the bad news (saltier water) with the good news in the previous sentence (faster refilling), so it belongs at the end of the first clause and takes a comma before it. The text after the blank, 'chloride readings...had doubled,' is a second complete sentence, so a semicolon has to follow 'though.'

A.why: You put the strong break before the transition, as you would with 'however.' But 'though chloride readings...had doubled since monitoring began' is a dependent clause. Starting with 'though' turns it into a fragment, and a fragment can't follow a semicolon.

B.why: You set 'though' off correctly but left the two complete sentences joined by a comma alone. That is a comma splice.

D.why: With no punctuation, 'though' becomes a subordinating conjunction: the water grew saltier even though chloride doubled. But rising chloride is what makes the water saltier, so that sentence calls the cause a contradiction.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Most scholars assume that the composer wrote his only symphony in movement order, beginning with the slow introduction. His surviving sketchbooks, which a nineteenth-century bookbinder reassembled in the wrong sequence after the composer's ______ suggest that the finale's main theme was drafted before any other material.
explanation: The comma after 'sketchbooks' opens an interruption, the 'which' clause, and the blank is where that interruption has to close. Cross it out: 'His surviving sketchbooks...suggest that the finale's main theme was drafted first.' That is a single sentence with subject 'sketchbooks' and verb 'suggest.' A comma closes the 'which' clause, and 'however' then interrupts the main clause before the verb, so it needs a comma after it as well.

A.why: You saw 'however' and reached for a semicolon. But 'His surviving sketchbooks, which...after the composer's death' is a subject without its verb, and 'however, suggest that...' has no subject. There is a fragment on each side of the semicolon.

B.why: The interruption opened with a comma after 'sketchbooks,' so it has to close with a comma. A dash at the closing end doesn't match the opening mark.

C.why: A semicolon after 'however' still separates the subject 'sketchbooks' from its verb 'suggest,' which leaves two fragments. The 'which' clause is also never closed with a comma.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Eighteenth-century merchants promoted block-printed calico as an affordable substitute for imported silk. The calico was indeed cheap to ______ washed out after only a few launderings, and buyers who had expected the durability of silk often returned it.
explanation: 'The calico was indeed cheap to produce' is a complete sentence, and so is 'its colours...washed out,' so a semicolon goes between them. 'However' marks the contrast between cheap production and colours that wash out, so it belongs in the second clause. It sits between that clause's subject and verb, so it needs a comma on each side.

B.why: You placed 'however' correctly, but only a comma separates the two complete sentences. That is a comma splice.

C.why: The comma after 'however' has no matching comma before it. That leaves a single comma between the subject 'its colours' and the verb 'washed,' which is a point where no comma can go.

D.why: Putting 'however' at the end of the first clause sets it against the previous sentence. But 'The calico was indeed cheap' confirms the merchants' claim. 'Indeed' tells you it agrees, so there is no contrast there. The contrast comes with the faded colours.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: In 2016 the county raised its minimum wage by a third (the steepest single increase anywhere in the ______ even so, employment among workers aged 16 to 19 changed by less than one percent over the following two years, according to payroll records.
explanation: This takes two steps. First, the parenthesis that opened before 'the steepest' has to close right after 'state,' because 'even so' doesn't belong to the aside. Second, the main clause 'the county raised its minimum wage by a third' is complete, and so is 'employment...changed by less than one percent.' So a semicolon goes after the closing parenthesis, and 'even so,' starts the second clause.

A.why: You found the boundary but put it inside the parentheses. That pulls 'even so' into the aside, and the main clause has no real break before 'employment' begins a new sentence.

B.why: You closed the parenthesis correctly but then joined two complete sentences with commas around 'even so.' That is a comma splice. 'Even so' is not a conjunction, so it can't do the joining.

C.why: Nothing separates the two complete sentences after the parenthesis, which makes this a run-on. The comma after 'even so' doesn't create a boundary.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Folklorists long assumed that the tale of the clever miller reached the interior from coastal ports, carried inland by sailors and traders. Its oldest written versions point ______ every one of them is set in a mountain village, and none so much as mentions the sea.
explanation: 'Its oldest written versions point elsewhere' contrasts with the folklorists' coastal theory, so 'however' belongs at the end of that clause, after a comma. That clause is complete and points forward to a 'where.' The next clause answers it: every version is set in a mountain village. A colon is the mark that delivers that explanation.

A.why: This is the trap that remains after you've found the boundary. Starting the second clause with 'however' says the mountain settings contrast with 'point elsewhere,' but they are the evidence for it. The contrast is with the earlier assumption.

C.why: Commas around 'however' can't separate two complete sentences, so this is a comma splice.

D.why: The colon is in the right place, but putting 'however' after it again sets the mountain villages against 'point elsewhere,' when they support it. That also leaves the actual contrast, with the coastal theory, unmarked.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Because no damaging earthquake had struck it in recorded history, the Varden Fault was long classified as inactive. Trenching across its trace in 2021 exposed sand blows left by at least four prehistoric ______ could no longer be treated as a negligible hazard by regional planners.
explanation: 'Trenching...exposed sand blows left by at least four prehistoric earthquakes' is a complete sentence. So is 'the fault...could no longer be treated as a negligible hazard,' and a semicolon goes between them. The new classification follows from the trenching evidence, so 'therefore' belongs to the second clause. It sits between that clause's subject and verb, so it needs a comma on each side.

A.why: You placed 'therefore' correctly, but the two complete sentences are joined by a comma alone. That is a comma splice.

B.why: Attaching 'therefore' to the first clause says the trenching discoveries were a result of the fault being classified as inactive. They weren't. The reclassification is what follows from the evidence.

D.why: The comma after 'therefore' has no matching comma before it, so a single comma falls between the subject 'the fault' and its verb 'could.'
